question: Mary chose an even \(4\)-digit number \(n.\) She wrote down all the divisors of \(n\) in increasing order from left to right: \(1,\) \(2,\) \(\ldots,\) \(\tfrac{n}{2},\) \(n.\) At some moment Mary wrote \(323\) as a divisor of \(n.\) What is the smallest possible value of the next divisor written to the right of \(323?\)
solution:
Two coprime divisors have their product dividing \(n\), which would be too large here. To use this restriction, let \(d\) be any divisor of \(n\) greater than \(323\), and set \(g=\gcd(d,323)\).

If \(g=1\), then \(323d\) divides \(n\). But
\[
n\ge323d>323^2=104329>9999,
\]
contradicting the four-digit condition. Therefore \(g>1\).

Since \(323=17\cdot19\), every divisor of \(323\) greater than \(1\) is at least \(17\), so \(g\ge17\). Also, \(g\) divides the positive integer \(d-323\). Hence
\[
d-323\ge g\ge17,
\qquad d\ge340.
\]
This bound can be attained. Choose
\[
n=17\cdot19\cdot20=6460.
\]
This is an even four-digit number, and both \(323\) and \(340=17\cdot20\) divide it. The bound above rules out every divisor strictly between them, so \(340\) is the next divisor after \(323\).

The smallest possible next divisor is \(\boxed{340}\), choice \(\text{C}\).
